title: Ridgley's view of the union and recording-session delegates
summary: He thinks unions have outlived usefulness; Tad recalls delegates sitting in on sessions, and Mr. Green stopping recordings.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: What about your dealings with 496 over the years? What did you do about it?

496, well, they had me before the boat every other week. Well, for failing to file a contract. I didn't do this yet. You know, and I thought there was a bunch of dogs. In fact, the union as a whole, I think, you know, people, a lot of people get on me when I say this because there are people who are strictly unionized. I'm not unionized. I feel like we can get, we can make it without the union because, because what the union do for them? I think the unions have outlived their usefulness. I think it's, I think that, you can forget about the union, not because everybody know about how much money they deserve to make, and just as a whole. And I think people know just about what they're supposed to pay. And I don't need no man to buy to come in and say so and so and so is the case, and now you bring me some of your money, because that's all the union does. Yeah.
Well, the union, I heard they were notorious years ago. They would sit on your session. Mm-hm.
I heard they were notorious years ago, they would sit on each session.

Oh, oh, they had a delegate, Mr. Green. Mr. Green was a delegate. He would come around there and, you know, you would record. He would come there, but if people didn't look right, he would stop it. Stop the recording session. But no, he wasn't.
